entries.text: Experience design is, after all, the design of experience, not appearance.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: On the Serengeti, Rohde’s team saw that its power came from seeing everything at once, which a theme park could never reproduce. They switched to a smaller, hillier reserve that could be translated. When your medium can’t capture a reference’s essence, choose another reference.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde treats space like colour: it is perceived relative to its surroundings. Guests start the safari in a cramped, walled town, so the savanna feels huge, even though it is smaller than the car park.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The safari’s ‘open’ savanna is really a series of separate rooms of trees and earth, arranged like scenes that open out and then close down again. What looks natural is tightly structured underneath.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde contrasts two geometries. Organisations map known goals with fixed points and lines; creative work grows outward from a motive, like a fractal. You can’t chart a route to something that doesn’t exist yet.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A fractal keeps producing detail forever, and every layer is tempting. A creative team has to decide when to stop generating, so that one version can be measured and built. Planning takes over only after that point.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde bristles at ‘theme’ used as a verb, as if it were decoration stuck onto a surface. For him a theme is a noun: the underlying idea that organises every decision in a complex project.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A single word like ‘freedom’ is too vague to be a theme. A useful theme statement both gives a reason to act and sets a standard for judging the results, so the team can sense the project before it exists.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: To build a theme, Rohde asks three things: what values sit under this project, why they are the right choice, and how they can be expressed so both the makers and the audience understand them.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Top-down command is too slow for a big creative project, and nobody can predict the next order. A shared theme lets each contributor make their own decisions that still fit the whole.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Once a theme exists, Rohde says, nobody owns it. Team members needn’t personally believe its values, only commit to them for the project, which takes the ego and ownership friction out of collaboration.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Without a clear theme, projects are just random collections of things.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde calls a big kickoff brainstorm a strategic mistake. Stories get made by two to six people; only once the theme and story are coherent should the team grow, because newcomers then join something with momentum.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Every executive review of Animal Kingdom began with the park’s themes restated before any idea was shown. Reviewers judged each proposal against agreed principles, not personal taste.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Conservationists had no interest in theme parks but cared deeply about the park’s theme. Working from that shared value produced attractions, such as a rafting story about illegal logging, that designers alone would never have reached.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: After proposing a theme, test it on hypothetical cases. If it keeps producing good answers, the team develops a useful bias: everyone starts spotting fitting opportunities without being told what is right.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: We are not all geniuses, but we might manufacture one single genius through collaboration.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In a market, Rohde rejected a braided finger ring until the seller said it would be an earring once it was in his ear. Rohde had been looking for something already in his head instead of transforming what was in front of him.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Things are not what they are. They are what they can do.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: To think laterally, forget an object’s name and list its properties. A chair has four legs like a dog; dogs are loyal; so a chair could become a walking robot that follows someone and lets them sit when they tire.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Developing an experience for Virgin Galactic, Rohde’s group set aside the ‘final frontier’ idea of staring out into space. Passengers look back at Earth, so the story became the return: coming home changed, with something to share.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says magicians amaze us using perfectly ordinary physics; the magic lies in what we expected. Keep the audience feeling they half-know where things are going but can’t quite predict how.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde warns against simply asking people what they want and handing it over. Creative work should turn expectation around, delivering a surprise that seems perfect and inevitable afterwards.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Without surprise, there is no attention.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A goal makes the ending predictable, and energy drops once people can see whether it will be reached, like fans leaving a decided game. A theme is open-ended: it guides from the start and keeps the team curious.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For a Coachella stage, Rohde’s team first built a favela set that looked like immovable concrete, then transformed it several times. First make the audience believe nothing can change, then change it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Logic is refutable. Metaphor is viral.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A simile (‘like a leopard’) invites the audience to weigh similarities and differences. A metaphor (‘the engine snarls and pounces’) lands before they can argue. Rohde uses metaphor to make an abstract theme concrete.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A built place can’t state its ideas the way a novel does; it has to speak through metaphor. Rohde wants music, aromas, textures, colours and script to act as metaphors for one another, all expressing the same theme.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Handed a roller coaster for a nature park, Rohde’s team swapped the brief ‘build a coaster’ for ‘use a coaster to express the theme’. Rohde’s earlier reading said the yeti guards wild places, so the yeti attacks the train.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: On Pandora, the theme statement guided everything from the screw holding a light to the volume and composition of the music. Because every designer knew the intent, the team could work on its own in parallel.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Once the Pandora theme was clear, Rohde’s job shifted from giving orders to editing. Designers stopped asking what to do; they showed him what they had already done and asked for critique.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde shows how theme works as a chain of likelihoods: a place about the value of nature implies organic landscape, eroded buildings, rough wooden doors, tarnished knobs. Anyone following the chain can invent a fitting chair unaided.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A good theme is predictable without being prescriptive: whatever it doesn’t rule out is probably fine. That turns every team member into a driver rather than a dozing passenger.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Settle the unifying theme before the flood of input arrives. Without it, people have no way to sort the incoming ideas; with it, they can all drive, and let each other drive.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Direction must come before action.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A designer still shaken by street poverty seen on a research trip chose a white for a ruined palace that made the finished set feel depressing. Rohde rescued it with a rose glaze over everything.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde treats the crew’s emotional state as a material: no contract or review caught the sadness that crept into one design until it was built. Managing feelings belongs beside schedule, budget and scope.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Feeding a crew well tells them what’s expected of them. Rohde’s construction partner shipped in crawdads, not burgers, because an ordinary meal signals an ordinary team being asked for extraordinary work.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde admits he neglects emotional care, so he leaned on producers for it and took a different role: guarding the perimeter, absorbing political hits and running interference so the team’s stress wasn’t compounded by chaos.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: To create, people need to feel safe.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde suggests replacing loaded words like ‘exciting’ or ‘elegant’ with nonsense pairs like maluma and takete, which only carry a feeling. Then flip it: if the project is takete, list how it could be maluma.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A plan, Rohde says, is only a theory based on what you know today, and tomorrow you’ll know more. You need one to start, it won’t survive contact, and each step forward needs a fresh one.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When his canvases were pre-tinted for autumn and it snowed the first night, Rohde painted anyway, reasoning that if he proved it possible in a blizzard, anything else would be too.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde keeps four questions in view while a project shifts: why must this be done, how will I know it’s finished, how does today relate to the original plan, and what must happen today.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Pursue the right expression, not the original one. If theme and purpose drive you rather than a fixed destination, what you stumble on may beat what you set out for.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Don’t wait for the right moment. Make the moment right.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: On the Adventurers Club, Rohde’s naturalistic performers were so convincing guests couldn’t tell they were actors, which read as creepy, not welcoming. He concluded he’d been too timid; characters had to be broad enough to signal ‘show’.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Immersive experiences only work if people can set their own level of involvement. The club let watchers stay on the balcony, joiners go downstairs, and the bold enter small rooms for close interaction.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The club’s hidden puppeteer cavities came from two unrelated memories: a cluttered London museum and the skewed rooms of a ghost novel Rohde read as a teen. Old references can resurface as practical solutions.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When the brief kept shifting, Rohde kept asking ‘What are we trying to do here?’ The answers evolved until he found the real theme: not adventure, but belonging.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Hold tight to a thread that leads back to the beginning.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde distinguishes co-laboration, working side by side toward a shared result, from ‘sub-laboration’, working for someone toward a conclusion already decided. Only the first produces outcomes nobody could have predicted.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Painting a mural with Inuit communities, Rohde set his own opinions aside and acted as a skilled pair of hands. The result was nothing he would have made alone, and he found that thrilling.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde’s first Tree of Life sketch was a modest 40-foot banyan. As creative director he could have forced it back to his comfort zone; instead experts kept escalating it, and the final tree far outperformed his idea.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Model-shop carvers proposed sculpting animals in relief instead of Rohde’s timid incised lines. He feared the cost; they knew their craft and assured him the difference was negligible. Trust specialists on what their own craft costs.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A goal is a by-product of the motive. Lead by the theme rather than the target, so that a new opportunity isn’t squeezed into an opinion formed before any real work was done.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The purpose of collaboration is discovery, not command.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde pictures a creative team as a solar system: the theme sits at the centre, with passionate advocates nearest, professionals further out and doubters at the edge, free to voice concerns all the way inward.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde made a habit of asking ‘Why is this a good idea, and how does it flow from the theme?’ before giving his view. Soon everyone interrogated each other, him included, and rationale preceded opinion.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: If you hold authority, you may have to beg colleagues to argue with you until they get used to it, and then accept living with the arguments.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A leader’s task is to multiply leaders.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde distrusts consensus: it is usually coerced by fear of exclusion, and merely announcing you want it frames disagreement as disloyal. Aim instead for a clear spread of opinion from advocacy to dissent.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For the Avatar ride, Rohde wanted a mid-ride pause of stillness and darkness so the climax would land; his producer said it would feel broken. The compromise: slowing almost to a stop, with the creature’s breathing filling the moment.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde backed leaning arches over floating mountains because they seemed feasible. Engineering showed the arches were just as hard and costly. The cautious option isn’t automatically the cheap one; test it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde separates three things: critique judges whether the work meets its goal, dissent questions the direction itself, and opposition just wants you to stop. Welcome the first two; make opponents work as hard as you.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In ‘triadic negotiation’ nobody owns the idea; it is set aside as a third party and judged only on how well it serves the theme and intended effect, which keeps debate impersonal.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A key question for any proposal: what does it hinge on, and how will that central idea be protected as it passes through production? Also: why do you believe the audience will receive it as you intend?

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Dissent is a form of participation.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A trend line is an abstraction; only the data points are real, and none may sit on the line. Creative people can bet on outliers, like six-clawed cats, ignoring the interpretation rather than the data.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When every beachfront hotel is forced into the same shape by law and economics, Rohde says the difference must come from meaning, not structure: the dance, not the dancer standing still.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Facing an immovable deadline on the Guardians of the Galaxy ride, Rohde’s team designed the attraction around the schedule: every part had to stand alone with no cross-dependencies, and a list of what to cut was agreed before work began.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Staring at the Tower of Terror, Rohde asked how many details actually made it read as a hotel. Very few. Strip them and the mass could be a prison or a power plant; a thing is only what we say it is.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Because people filter what they tell bosses, leaders get the least reliable information. Rohde always took a sub-role on his projects where he reported to someone who reported to him.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: No” is a lazy answer.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde argues a creative project should not try to predict its outcome; each day should be a discovery. But to be genuinely unpredictable, you first have to know exactly what the predicted result would be.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For Aulani, Rohde’s team pinned up rival resorts’ marketing images and removed every redundant cliché. What survived, the specific local people, became the theme. Delete the generic and see what remains.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Aulani’s art carries almost no explanatory labels, so curious guests must ask the Hawaiian staff. Withholding the explanation turned the design into a prompt for real conversation about the culture.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Skeptical Hawaiian artists joined Aulani only because the team could state its thematic purpose clearly. ‘Building a hotel’ was not an answer; a cultural reason was. Your purpose recruits collaborators.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Disruption is a by-product of poor organization.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde defines courage not as the absence of fear but as acting while afraid. The key, he says, is treating fear as a reaction rather than as a fact.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Our brains overweight vivid, painful outcomes. Rohde urges teams to judge risk with numbers, not emotion: how much pain, how likely, what cost. Otherwise survivable risks get vetoed.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Fear may be justified, but panic is not a strategy.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Creative work should be risky, not scary. Rohde says risk management exists not to block action but to answer one question: if this is where we must go, how do we get there safely?

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A leader must make others unafraid, not just be unafraid. Fear lives in the unknown, so Rohde puts the duty to dispel it first on whoever knows the most.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When Rohde stretched a designer into a far bigger role, he paired the assignment with concrete promises: mentoring, cover, extra staff if needed and plans for what might go wrong.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde calls managing by fear both a moral and a managerial error. Frightened people lie, hide or shut down, picking the fastest way out of fear rather than better work.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde observes that failure is often just nostalgia for the original plan. It sets new conditions for the next move, so play the ball where it lies.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Animal Kingdom’s winding, view-blocking paths overshot the adventure theme and confused guests. The fix was opening a sliver of sightline: the theme survived at a level people could embrace.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Persistence doesn’t always mean rebuilding the same thing. Rohde notes the Everest story needs a yeti that seems alive, not that particular machine, so a different solution might serve it better.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The answer to momentary failure is always to go back and address the motive.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In big ensembles, failure rarely traces to one person, and neither does success. Where failure is dangerous to careers, Rohde says energy goes into finger-pointing; forgiveness keeps people looking forward.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In Rohde’s one-pencil, one-sheet exercise, nobody claims the theme is impossible without more materials. A strong thematic motive, he argues, removes the perception of limitation entirely.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: There is no relationship between material limitations and the expression of a thematic idea.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says limitations are never the real problem. Trouble starts when a creative team lacks the power and autonomy to transform the limitations it has been given.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Don’t wait for full consensus before moving. Rohde pictures paradise as a noisy room of people arguing hard, and warns that critics will still be along for the ride.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: With Animal Kingdom stalled in limbo, Rohde told the CEO he didn’t have to build it, but needed to decide, because the team was losing talent every day.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: After passing through many hands, a project eventually needs focus. Rohde calls it freezing the equation: keep the concepts that matter, cut redundancy, drop what the crew can’t produce.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Keep noodling and you risk passing the point where the work had shape and meaning. Because creatives work on impulse, Rohde says knowing when to stop takes training.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: An elegant solution is easy to break. A clear statement is easy to muddle.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde is spellbound by shadow puppets: flat silhouettes and voices holding audiences all night. It cannot be simpler, yet it works, so any extra you add had better be worth it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Passion drives work forward, but Rohde says dispassion tells you when it’s done. Early work defining theme gives an outside standard for judging with an innocent eye.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The aim isn’t to know what the audience wants, Rohde says, but to empathize until you want it too. Delivering only what people ask for is merely a design service.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says the real project is the one still running five years later. Audiences reveal how the work actually behaves, prompting a second wave of design after opening.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde led Animal Kingdom’s design but wasn’t its designer; much of it was new to him. On Pandora, a theme-driven process let teams direct themselves.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Things are what they do. Action is existence.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde admires the Balinese view that anything sacred must be done beautifully, however short-lived. Craft is a form of devotion, not a hedge against a temporary result.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says to separate the pursuit of quality from rewards. Do your best work, absorbed in the present; if it is cancelled, you won’t wonder whether you were the cause.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Profit can be the reward of creative work, Rohde argues, never its motive. He notes that Blade Runner and The Iron Giant disappointed at the box office and endured.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Structure should follow the product, Rohde argues, not the reverse. An existing organization wants to persist, while a creative ensemble must evolve, because the problem only emerges once design begins.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Efficiency is often irrelevant to creative work: the cheapest opera isn’t the finest. Bahamian Junkanoo floats are deliberately hard to build, so they demand and strengthen a community.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: We create not just art. We create ourselves.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde treats an ensemble as one virtual creative mind, with each member a function of it. That mind organizes around a story, not a person, and theme sits at its center.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Be clear and then be generous.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde describes direction as geometry: it defines the vector where future actions will succeed. Like driving directions, it leaves the receiver free to choose their own route.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: People struggle to start from nothing. Before a community painting, Rohde sketched one image he was willing to erase, just to spark conversation and build momentum.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says expeditions and projects alike must begin before the ground truth appears. Plan for contingencies and worst cases, then start walking and adjust to what the trail actually holds.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible
